## Statement
A binary string is **valid** if it never has two `1`s next to each other (`1010` is valid, `0110` is not).

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> list_valid(int n);     // all valid strings of length n, in lexicographic order
unsigned long long count_valid(int n);          // how many valid strings of length n (n <= 85)
```

- `list_valid`: generate the strings recursively, choosing one character at a time. Only try `1` when the previous character isn't `1`. n ≤ 16.
- `count_valid`: n goes up to 85, so you can't list them. Write a recursive count, and **memoise** it (or find the recurrence).

`count_valid(0) = 1`, because the empty string is valid.

**Input:** commands `list n` and `count n` until the end of input. `list` prints the count followed by the strings.

## Starter
```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

vector<string> list_valid(int n) { return {}; }
unsigned long long count_valid(int n) { return 0; }
```

## Driver
```cpp
int main() {
    string cmd; int n;
    while (cin >> cmd >> n) {
        if (cmd == "list") {
            auto v = list_valid(n);
            cout << v.size();
            for (auto& s : v) cout << ' ' << s;
            cout << '\n';
        } else cout << count_valid(n) << '\n';
    }
}
```

## Hints
- Build the string one character at a time: push, recurse, pop.
- Allow `'1'` only when the current string is empty or doesn't end in `'1'`. Try `'0'` first to get lexicographic order.
- For counting, the only thing that matters is how many characters are left and whether the last one was `1`. Memoise on those two values.

## Solution
**Generation** is choose → explore → un-choose. Trying `'0'` before `'1'` produces the strings in lexicographic order automatically.

**Counting.** The state is *(characters left, was the last character a 1?)*. Without memoisation the recursion tree is as large as the answer (about 1.6ⁿ). With it, there are only `2n` distinct states.

The counts come out as 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …: the Fibonacci numbers, because `count(n) = count(n−1) + count(n−2)`. Either the string ends in `0` (anything valid of length `n−1`, then `0`), or it ends in `01` (anything valid of length `n−2`, then `01`).

Complexity: listing is O(n · answer), and counting is O(n) with memoisation.

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

static void gen(string& cur, int n, vector<string>& out) {
    if ((int)cur.size() == n) { out.push_back(cur); return; }
    cur.push_back('0'); gen(cur, n, out); cur.pop_back();          // '0' is always allowed
    if (cur.empty() || cur.back() != '1') {                         // '1' only after a non-'1'
        cur.push_back('1'); gen(cur, n, out); cur.pop_back();
    }
}

vector<string> list_valid(int n) {
    vector<string> out; string cur;
    gen(cur, n, out);
    return out;
}

// ways(len, lastWasOne): number of ways to append `len` more characters
static unsigned long long memo[100][2];
static bool seen[100][2];
static unsigned long long ways(int len, int last1) {
    if (len == 0) return 1;
    if (seen[len][last1]) return memo[len][last1];
    unsigned long long r = ways(len - 1, 0);            // put a '0'
    if (!last1) r += ways(len - 1, 1);                  // put a '1'
    seen[len][last1] = true;
    return memo[len][last1] = r;
}

unsigned long long count_valid(int n) { return ways(n, 0); }
```
